steps.note: THE TEST: a recording now leaves the app through the same Export sheet a picture does, instead of a bare system save box with the format already decided. Format, then what the file will be, then what it will weigh, in the places the picture sheet puts them

THE NEW TEST: a video now has the same three choices the animated formats always had, and on a video they mean something the animated ones do not. High is the recording as it is and hands back the instant verbatim copy; Small caps the long side at 960 and spends a budget the app chose, so the line underneath answers 960 by 600 at 30 fps and the weight falls with it. Under the row, one sentence saying who the choice is for, because High and Small say which is bigger and nothing about which you want

GIF is one press away rather than a different menu item, and picking it grows the Quality row the submenu used to hold. THE NEW TEST: the line that used to say "size not known until it is written" now says what the GIF weighs. There is no formula for one, so the sheet writes the GIF into a scratch file while it is open, counts up as it goes, and says the size of the file that landed. That is why it is a plain number and not an "about": it is the file, and pressing Export saves that very file

Small asked for, and the line underneath answers 480 by 300 at 10 fps. The weight moves with it too, because the scratch GIF is written again at the new preset: the number on the sheet always belongs to the choice showing on the sheet

the third format, same sheet, same two lines, and a weight on it for the first time. All three are now reachable from one place instead of from three menu items, and all three say what the file will weigh
three formats and a preset tried on, then Cancel. The recording is still eight seconds, the file on disk is still eight seconds, and no original was preserved because nothing was ever committed

THE WAIT: a write long enough to notice is a card with a bar on it and the writer's own count of how far through it is, not a spinner the size of a fingernail inside the Export button. The window behind it carries on drawing, and there is one thing to do about it: Stop
Stop, and the half-written file goes with it. No folder full of files that play for two seconds

High on a recording nobody has touched is still a straight file copy: the same bytes, written in a handful of milliseconds, and the sheet's number is exact rather than an estimate. Exported a second time it is byte for byte the same file

the same untouched recording at Standard: a real encode, and the number the sheet promised before anybody committed to it is checked against the file that landed. This is the case the whole row exists for, because the commonest reason to export a recording nobody has edited is that the one on disk is too big to send

and Small, capped at 960 on the long side, which is what the line on the sheet said it would be. Written twice, it comes out the same size both times: a re-encode is not reproducible to the byte, because the system's own encoder decides differently under different load, but it does not change size on you

the same recording trimmed to its middle four seconds and cropped to the middle of its frame. The sheet says 640 by 400 px, 0:04 of 0:08, so what is about to be written is readable where it is about to be written. The weight says about, because a re-encode is an estimate and not a promise

THE OTHER TEST: the file really written, opened and measured. Four seconds not eight, 640 by 400 not 1280 by 800, so the trim and the crop reached the file rather than only the app. It is not a copy of the recording either, which is what proves the re-encode ran

the same edits out as an animated GIF at the Small preset. The crop is 640 by 400 and Small caps the long side at 480, so the frames land at 480 by 300: the preset is a cap rather than a size, and the crop is carried into the GIF as well as into the video

the same edits out as an animated HEIC. The number the sheet worked out by writing a scratch copy is held against the file that landed at nought per cent of drift allowed: an animated export written twice comes out the same size, which is what lets the sheet promise a size instead of an estimate
